definition: the deliberate giving up of something one has a right to, especially comfort or self-interest
examples: The order was founded on abnegation and silence.
His abnegation of authority surprised the committee.

definition: widely repeated but almost certainly not true
examples: The quotation is probably apocryphal.
Every profession keeps its apocryphal stories.

definition: strikingly well suited to the point being made
examples: She chose an apposite example.
The comparison is apposite rather than merely clever.

definition: showing steady and careful attention over a long period
examples: Her assiduous note-taking saved the project.
He was assiduous in checking every source.

definition: to give a false impression of something, or to show a claim to be untrue
examples: Her calm voice belied her nerves.
The figures belie the official account.

definition: to raise petty objections about small details
examples: Critics cavilled at the ending.
One might cavil at the title, but the argument holds.

definition: existing only in the imagination and impossible to achieve
examples: The scheme proved chimerical.
He pursued a chimerical certainty.

definition: moving from one thing to another without plan or steady purpose
examples: They made desultory conversation.
His reading was wide but desultory.

definition: slow to act, in a way that causes delay
examples: The office was dilatory in replying.
Dilatory tactics held up the vote.

definition: to free someone of a belief that is mistaken
examples: Let me disabuse you of that idea.
A week on site disabused him of his optimism.

definition: full of cheerful energy that is hard to contain
examples: She was ebullient after the result.
An ebullient crowd filled the square.

definition: to drain someone of energy or vitality
examples: The heat enervated everyone by noon.
Long meetings enervate more than they inform.

definition: understood by only a small group with special knowledge
examples: The debate turned esoteric.
He collects esoteric editions of grammar books.

definition: to make amends for a wrong one has done
examples: He spent years trying to expiate that failure.
No apology could expiate the harm.

definition: silly in a way that shows no awareness of how silly it is
examples: It was a fatuous suggestion.
He wore a fatuous smile through the whole meeting.

definition: to deny or contradict something, usually used in the negative
examples: There is no gainsaying her influence.
Few would gainsay the basic finding.

definition: a biography that treats its subject with uncritical admiration
examples: The memoir slides into hagiography.
Reviewers dismissed the book as hagiography.

definition: a person who attacks beliefs or institutions that others hold in respect
examples: She built a career as an iconoclast.
Every field needs its iconoclasts.

definition: impossible to escape or avoid, however one struggles
examples: The ineluctable arithmetic of the deadline.
Ageing is ineluctable; decline is not.

definition: actively harmful to something, or openly unfriendly
examples: Such secrecy is inimical to trust.
The climate is inimical to citrus.

definition: showing a relaxed lack of concern, sometimes where concern is warranted
examples: He gave an insouciant shrug.
Her insouciant tone irritated the panel.

definition: very hard to solve or control, and resistant to every attempt
examples: Housing remains an intractable problem.
The pain proved intractable.

definition: to speak or write against something with strong hostility
examples: He inveighed against the new rules for an hour.
Editorials inveighed against the decision.

definition: using very few words, in a way that can seem cool or dismissive
examples: His reply was laconic: two words.
She has a laconic wit.

definition: a gap where something expected is missing, especially in a text or an argument
examples: There is a lacuna in the manuscript.
The theory has an obvious lacuna.

definition: extremely generous in giving
examples: A munificent donor paid for the wing.
The offer was munificent by any standard.

definition: refusing to change one's mind however strong the argument against it
examples: The board remained obdurate.
He was obdurate on the one point that mattered.

definition: to remove a difficulty so that dealing with it becomes unnecessary
examples: The new design obviates the need for a second pump.
Careful wording obviates most disputes.

definition: done as a duty and without real interest or care
examples: He gave the report a perfunctory glance.
The apology was perfunctory.

definition: quick to notice and understand what is not obvious to others
examples: A perspicacious reader will see the flaw.
Her perspicacious questions unsettled him.

definition: to be a sign that something, usually bad, is going to happen
examples: The stillness presaged a storm.
Falling orders presaged the closure.

definition: to forbid something officially, often by law
examples: The practice was proscribed in 1908.
Certain compounds are proscribed outright.

definition: belonging to ordinary daily life, and therefore easy to overlook
examples: The poems dwell on quotidian detail.
Quotidian tasks filled the afternoon.

definition: dealing with a subject so obscure that few readers can follow it
examples: The footnotes are recondite even for specialists.
He wrote on recondite points of grammar.

definition: confident and hopeful, especially where others see difficulty
examples: She remains sanguine about the deadline.
Few economists were so sanguine.

definition: appearing sound at first glance but false once examined
examples: The argument is specious.
He offered a specious justification for the delay.

definition: behaving as though one were superior to everyone present
examples: He answered in a supercilious tone.
The clerk gave a supercilious smile.

definition: expressed with sharpness and force, and cutting to the heart of the matter
examples: She wrote a trenchant critique of the plan.
His trenchant questions ended the debate.

definition: quick to argue and eager for a fight
examples: The witness turned truculent under questioning.
A truculent silence filled the room.

definition: the quality of seeming true to life, whether or not it is true
examples: The dialogue has real verisimilitude.
Detail lends verisimilitude to the account.
